goal_text: I've already built an LLM app and want to understand agents

nodes.title: What makes something an "agent" vs. a prompt call?
nodes.one_liner: The shift from one-shot calls to a decide-act-observe loop.

nodes.title: The agent loop, concretely
nodes.one_liner: How reason → act → observe → repeat runs until done.

nodes.title: Giving the model tools
nodes.one_liner: Defining tools, function-calling, and passing results back.

nodes.title: Wire a first tool-using loop into your app
nodes.one_liner: Minimal working agent bolted onto your existing calls.

nodes.title: Managing state, memory, and context across steps
nodes.one_liner: What to keep in context and what to persist between turns.

nodes.title: Planning and multi-step reasoning strategies
nodes.one_liner: How the model breaks a task into steps and self-corrects.

nodes.title: Keeping the loop from going off the rails
nodes.one_liner: Step limits, error handling, timeouts, and cost control.

nodes.title: Observing, debugging, and evaluating your agent
nodes.one_liner: Tracing runs and knowing when the agent actually works.

nodes.title: Do you even need an agent here?
nodes.one_liner: When a plain call or fixed workflow beats a loop.

outline.rationale: The user is fluent in single prompt/completion calls and wants to build an agent into an existing app, so I skip prompting/API basics, framework surveys, and broad theory. The outline moves from the core conceptual shift (agent vs. call) to the mechanics of the loop and tools, then an early hands-on implementation node to satisfy the build endpoint. Later nodes cover the harder production realities (state/memory, planning, guardrails, observability) that separate a toy loop from something shippable. The final node injects a pragmatic decision check, valuable for someone who might over-apply agents where a simpler workflow suffices. Nodes are MECE-ish: loop mechanics, tools, state, planning, guardrails, and evaluation each answer distinct questions with low overlap.
